metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: when you ask Claude to close the month, is it using its own accounting judgment — or following a written file, the same way every time? Lands the carry-out that Claude runs the same four fixed steps on any input, and the edge of what it does is exactly the edge of what that file says.

beats.narration_text: Someone wondered if Claude would close the books using its own judgment. It doesn't — it follows a written skill file, step by step. So: can Claude close my books using a skill file?

beats.narration_text: A skill is a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one is called close-month, and its SKILL.md file is the instruction set — plain language, no hidden logic. Claude reads the file, then follows it. The file is the whole program.

The instructions run as a fixed pipeline. Reconcile the books against payment processors. Flag anything that doesn't match. Write a plain-language summary of the month. Export the finished packet. Each step runs in order — there's no improvising outside that list.

production_viz.label: FOUR FIXED STEPS
production_viz.caption: steps run in order, not by judgment

beats.narration_text: Run it twice on the same numbers and it does the same four steps both times — same input, same output. That reliability has one edge: it only does what those steps say. Anything the file doesn't cover, it doesn't do.

production_viz.label: RELIABLE, AND ONLY THAT WIDE
production_viz.caption: reliable, and only as wide as the file

beats.narration_text: Claude doesn't improvise the close — it runs the same written steps every time, on any numbers you give it. The edge of what it does is exactly the edge of what that file says.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I want to close the month — reconcile QuickBooks against payment processors, flag anything that doesn't match, write a P&L narrative, and export the close packet. Read the close-month skill first, and walk me through what you'll do before you do it. That last part matters — asking Claude to explain itself first is how you catch a bad step before it runs.
